clue.text: Old Nick of London

parts.note: nick is slang for a prison, so an old nick in London is a former jail there, not the devil

explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Nick' looks like the devil, but 'nick' is British slang for a prison; NEWGATE was London's notorious old jail.
explanation.definitionFit: Newgate Prison was the capital's most famous historic jail, demolished in 1904.

clue.text: Found in cell, eccentric uncle's round the bend

indicators.note: round means the scrambled relative goes around the bend
eccentric means odd or off-centre, so the letters are rearranged

parts.note: a U-shaped bend gives the letter U

explanation.surface: An odd uncle, locked up in a cell, has gone mad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'eccentric' shuffles UNCLES into NUCLES, and 'round' puts it around U. 'Round the bend' looks like British slang for mad.
explanation.definitionFit: The central body of a living cell, holding its genetic material.

clue.text: Light horticulture?

parts.note: light here is a pane or opening in a house wall, so this is gardening on a sill or ledge

explanation.walkthrough: 'Light' looks like 'easy', but a light is a window.
explanation.definitionFit: Growing plants in boxes on a sill is a form of cultivation.

clue.text: There is nothing in beer to make a bitter sort

indicators.note: in places the zero inside the drink

parts.note: ale is a type of beer
nothing is zero, the letter O

explanation.surface: A drinker finds no beer to make a bitter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bitter' looks like the beer, but it means bitter-tasting: the plant's sap is famously bitter.
explanation.definitionFit: This succulent plant yields a bitter juice once used as a purgative.

clue.text: Coats provided by seamen?

annotationWithheld.why: Coats provided by seamen?: SEAMEN rearranges to only six of the seven letters, with no word to give the L and no anagram signal, and no cryptic reading has been found; no scan or blog to settle it.

clue.text: Steal a bit for a jumper, perhaps

definitions.text: a bit for a jumper, perhaps

explanation.surface: A rider pinches a piece of tack for a show-jumping horse.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumper' looks like a sweater, but it is a horse that jumps; a bit is the mouthpiece of its bridle.
explanation.definitionFit: To pilfer something is to snaffle it, and a snaffle is also a simple jointed bridle mouthpiece for a horse.

clue.text: Lively party in Nether Wallop?

parts.note: nether means lower, and the shin is on the lower leg
a wallop is a blow, a dig

explanation.surface: A rowdy celebration held in a Hampshire village.
explanation.walkthrough: Nether Wallop is a real village in Hampshire, England; split up, the name gives a lower body part and a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A noisy, lively celebration is a shindig.

clue.text: Pimpled features shellac never shows

indicators.note: shows means the letters are on display within the words that come before

explanation.surface: Varnish never reveals spotty skin.
explanation.definitionFit: A skin condition marked by spots and pustules.

clue.text: Mechanical Post-Impressionist?

parts.note: a device that impresses a stamp on mail, so it is a mechanical printer for the post

explanation.walkthrough: 'Post-Impressionist' looks like an art movement; read as 'post impressionist', it is a device stamping letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A device that prints postage marks on envelopes instead of stamps.

clue.text: Mere lad upset Beryl

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters are jumbled

explanation.surface: A mere boy annoyed a woman called Beryl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Beryl' looks like a woman's name, but beryl is a mineral.
explanation.definitionFit: The green gemstone is a variety of the mineral beryl.

clue.text: Athletics event bringing comfort to the nation?

parts.note: comfort given to someone sad is consolation
a nation or people can be called a race

explanation.surface: A sporting fixture that cheers up the whole country.
explanation.definitionFit: A consolation race is a contest held for runners eliminated from the main heats.

clue.text: Bishop of the borough

indicators.note: of says the letters are taken out of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A churchman serving a town's diocese.
explanation.walkthrough: EBOR, short for Eboracum (Latin for York), is the signature of the Archbishop of York.
explanation.definitionFit: The Archbishop of York signs himself by this Latin abbreviation of his see.

clue.text: Nurses having ambition in extremes of tenderness

indicators.note: in places the aim inside the pair of outer letters
the extremes of a word are its first and last letters only

parts.note: an ambition is an end you strive for

explanation.surface: Carers whose goal is to be as tender as they can.
explanation.definitionFit: To nurse a patient is to look after or care for them.

clue.text: This big gull repels other birds

indicators.note: repels means drives back, so the birds' name is turned back to front

parts.note: auks are diving seabirds such as puffins and guillemots

explanation.surface: A large gull drives off a flock of rival seabirds.
explanation.definitionFit: Skuas are large predatory seabirds of the gull family that rob other birds of food.

clue.text: Civic centre paid out for flat

indicators.note: the centre of a five-letter word is its third letter
out means disordered, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A town hall pays for an apartment.
explanation.definitionFit: Dull and lifeless is a sense of flat and vapid.

clue.text: Marriage needs welcoming feature at church

parts.note: a welcome mat is at the front door

explanation.surface: A wedding needs a welcome at the church.
explanation.definitionFit: A union of two people, as in a good match.

clue.text: Tokens for Telegraphs, say

explanation.surface: The newspaper's coupons promote its own title.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Telegraphs' looks like the paper's name, but it is a verb: to telegraph is to send a message.
explanation.definitionFit: Signs or indications are signals, and to communicate by telegraph is to send messages or signal.

clue.text: Having the appearance of a wood around Reading

annotationWithheld.why: Having the appearance of a wood around Reading: no newspaper scan; 'around Reading' would put R inside something, but no clue word gives GAINED or any other outer piece, so the clue as held looks garbled.
annotationWithheld.clue: Having the appearance of a wood around Reading

clue.text: Packer put me in-to partner Close?

definitions.text: Packer put me in-to partner Close?

parts.words: Packer put me in-to partner Close?
parts.note: a canning packer squeezes this small fish tightly in beside its neighbour, packed close together in a tin

explanation.surface: A team owner picks a player to bat alongside Brian Close.
explanation.walkthrough: The capitals suggest cricket (Kerry Packer, Brian Close), but the packer is a canner and 'close' is the cramped tin.
explanation.definitionFit: Small oily fish canned tightly side by side; 'packed like' these fish means crowded.

clue.text: An Armstrong rested, with companion, on near side of moon

parts.note: sat means rested
CH stands for Companion of Honour

indicators.note: the near side is the first half of the word

explanation.surface: Neil Armstrong sat down with a colleague on the moon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'near side of' takes MO, the first half of 'moon'. Armstrong suggests Neil, but this is jazz trumpeter Louis Armstrong's nickname.
explanation.definitionFit: Jazz trumpeter Louis Armstrong was nicknamed Satchmo.

clue.text: What's the matter in the pleura?

definitions.text: What's the matter in the pleura?

parts.words: What's the matter in the pleura?
parts.note: matter here is pus, collected in the membrane around the lungs

explanation.walkthrough: 'What's the matter' reads as 'what's wrong', but matter means pus.
explanation.definitionFit: A collection of pus in a body cavity, especially around the lungs.

clue.text: Recurring medical trouble?

indicators.note: trouble means a disturbance, so the letters are stirred up

explanation.surface: A medical complaint that keeps coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Recurring' is the definition by way of the phrase 'recurring decimal', a fraction whose digits repeat for ever.
explanation.definitionFit: A recurring number is a decimal in which a digit or group repeats endlessly.

clue.text: Debate — infernal position to place Orient

parts.note: Dis is the underworld, the infernal city in Dante
to put is to place
the Orient is the East, E

explanation.surface: An argument over where hell should stand relative to the East.
explanation.definitionFit: An argument or controversy is a dispute.

clue.text: Climbing-frames left by totters

parts.note: people who tot up sums are adders

explanation.surface: Playground equipment abandoned by wobbling toddlers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'totters' reads as people who wobble; here it means people who tot up, counting numbers.
explanation.definitionFit: Frames with rungs used for climbing up.

clue.text: Members at grass-roots level

parts.note: members are limbs or digits, and the ones at ground level touch the grass beneath our feet

explanation.surface: Ordinary party members working in local branches.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Members' and 'grass-roots' suggest a political party; here they are body parts standing on the lawn.
explanation.definitionFit: The digits on the feet are parts of the body that rest on the ground.

clue.text: Fit and well, sergeant-major!

parts.note: a spa is a mineral spring or well

explanation.surface: Someone tells the drill sergeant he is in good health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fit and well' reads as healthy, but 'Fit' is a noun, a sudden seizure.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden convulsion or attack is a fit.

clue.text: Kids favour such a drop in a police force

parts.note: CID is the Criminal Investigation Department of British police

explanation.surface: Children like a sweet handed out at the police station.
explanation.walkthrough: An acid drop is a sharp-tasting British boiled sweet; CID is the plain-clothes detective branch of British police.
explanation.definitionFit: Tart boiled sweets called acid drops are a children's favourite.

clue.text: Ring swan in public

parts.note: a ring is round, the letter O
a pen is a female swan

explanation.surface: A ringed swan displayed to the public.
explanation.definitionFit: Done openly, without secrecy, is done in public.

clue.text: This is the point of fencing

definitions.text: This is the point of fencing

parts.words: This is the point of fencing
parts.note: the point is the sword's tip, the weapon used in fencing bouts

explanation.walkthrough: 'the point of' reads as 'the purpose of', but means the tip of a sword.
explanation.definitionFit: A sword with a sharp point used in the sport of fencing.

clue.text: He will succeed if there are no further deliveries

definitions.text: He will succeed if there are no further deliveries

parts.words: He will succeed if there are no further deliveries
parts.note: deliveries are births: the next in line inherits only if no closer child is born

explanation.surface: A bowler or postman who triumphs once the last delivery is done.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Deliveries' suggests post or cricket balls; it means births of children who would take precedence in the line of succession.
explanation.definitionFit: One expected to inherit a title unless a nearer relative is born displaces them.

clue.text: Transparent, silky stuff piped from South Africa

parts.note: an organ is the instrument sounded through pipes
ZA is the international vehicle code for South Africa

explanation.surface: Fine sheer fabric shipped in by pipeline from South Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: 'piped' stands for the piped instrument, and ZA comes from the Afrikaans Zuid-Afrika.
explanation.definitionFit: This thin, stiff sheer fabric is made of silk or synthetic fibre.

clue.text: Teams-ones in pairs?

explanation.surface: Squads made up of players in twos.
explanation.walkthrough: Two ones side by side make the figure 11; cricket and football teams have this many players.
explanation.definitionFit: Cricket and football sides are each named for their number of players, and two ones written together read as that number.
